case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that the Due Process Clause forbids a State to terminate parental rights on a preponderance of the evidence and requires proof by at least clear and convincing evidence.
key_cases.relevance: Santosky sets the constitutional floor South Carolina applies in every TPR case, requiring each statutory ground under S.C. Code § 63-7-2570 to be proved by clear and convincing evidence.
key_cases.quote: Evaluation of the three Eldridge factors compels the conclusion that use of a "fair preponderance of the evidence" standard in such proceedings is inconsistent with due process.

key_cases.case_name: Lassiter v. Department of Social Services of Durham County
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that due process does not require appointment of counsel for an indigent parent in every termination proceeding, leaving the question to the trial court case by case subject to appellate review.
key_cases.relevance: Lassiter is the federal constitutional baseline for appointed counsel in TPR, and South Carolina has legislated above it — a point a practitioner must pair with S.C. Code § 63-7-2560(A) as construed in Broom.
key_cases.quote: neither can we say that the Constitution requires the appointment of counsel in every parental termination proceeding

key_cases.case_name: South Carolina Department of Social Services v. Sarah W.
key_cases.holding: The court upheld the 15-of-22-months ground as facially constitutional and reinstated termination, holding that the ground requires both a best-interests finding and that the delay in reunification be attributable to the parent rather than to the State.
key_cases.relevance: This is the leading South Carolina Supreme Court construction of the ASFA-derived 15-of-22-months TPR ground in S.C. Code § 63-7-2570(8).
key_cases.quote: section 63-7-2570(8) may not be used to sever parental rights based solely on the fact that the child has spent fifteen of the past twenty-two months in foster care

key_cases.case_name: S.C. Dep't of Soc. Servs. v. Smith
key_cases.holding: The court held that foster parents are interested parties with statutory standing to petition for TPR, found clear and convincing evidence that an incarcerated father willfully failed to visit and that his post-petition contacts were judicially motivated, and held termination was in the child's best interest.
key_cases.relevance: It is the controlling recent treatment of willfulness for an incarcerated parent and of curative conduct begun only after a TPR petition is filed.
key_cases.quote: Even if Foster Parents did not have standing to bring their private adoption action, it was well within Foster Parents' statutory right to file their TPR action.

key_cases.case_name: South Carolina Department of Social Services v. M.R.C.L.
key_cases.holding: The court reversed the Court of Appeals and reinstated termination, holding DSS proved by clear and convincing evidence that the mother willfully failed to support the child and that termination was in the child's best interest.
key_cases.relevance: M.R.C.L. is the Supreme Court's controlling application of the willful-failure-to-support ground and of appellate fact-finding in TPR appeals.
key_cases.quote: We find the Court of Appeals erred in holding DSS failed to show by clear and convincing evidence that mother willfully failed to support child.

key_cases.case_name: South Carolina Department of Social Services v. Michelle G.
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed termination, holding the mother lacked standing to attack S.C. Code § 63-7-2570(1) as void for vagueness because her own conduct fell squarely within the statute, and that the grounds and best-interests findings were supported by clear and convincing evidence.
key_cases.relevance: Michelle G. forecloses generalized vagueness attacks on South Carolina's TPR grounds and confirms the expedited appellate posture of TPR appeals.
key_cases.quote: Because her conduct clearly falls within the parameters of the statute, she lacks standing to challenge the statute as being void for vagueness.
